title: The Fox and the Crow
originalTitle: Ἀλώπηξ καὶ κόραξ · Alōpēx kai korax
place: An olive grove in ancient Greece
sourceAuthor: Aesop; selected and retold by Joseph Jacobs
note: A reading copy of Joseph Jacobs’s public-domain text. Line wrapping and page divisions are editorial; the verse following the prose fable in this edition is omitted.

rights.basis: The 1894 source edition is identified as public domain in the United States by Project Gutenberg.

artLabel: A fox flatters a crow holding cheese in an olive tree.

pageArt.alt: Crow opens her beak to sing as the cheese begins to fall toward Fox in the olive grove.
Fox carries away the cheese while Crow watches from the olive branch above.

scenes: A Fox once saw a Crow fly off with a piece of cheese in its beak and settle on a branch of a tree. “That’s for me, as I am a Fox,” said Master Reynard, and he walked up to the foot of the tree.

“Good-day, Mistress Crow,” he cried. “How well you are looking to-day: how glossy your feathers; how bright your eye. I feel sure your voice must surpass that of other birds, just as your figure does; let me hear but one song from you that I may greet you as the Queen of Birds.”

The Crow lifted up her head and began to caw her best, but the moment she opened her mouth the piece of cheese fell to the ground, only to be snapped up by Master Fox. “That will do,” said he. “That was all I wanted. In exchange for your cheese I will give you a piece of advice for the future—
